Root: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ — every subfolder with a SKILL.md (skip `_shared`, `synced`, any archive folder). Also note any project-level skills under C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\*\.claude\skills\ (depth 1-2).

Think-in-Code: program the analysis, do not compute it by reading raw data into your conversation.
  </priority_instructions>

  <deferred_tool_bootstrap>
    The context-mode tools below may be DEFERRED in your harness — their schemas are not loaded yet, so calling them directly fails (e.g. "tool not found" / InputValidationError). Load them ONCE before your first ctx_* call:

    After that they are callable. If any ctx_* call fails as not-found, ToolSearch it and retry — do NOT fall back to Bash/Read just because the schema was not loaded yet.
  </deferred_tool_bootstrap>

  <tool_selection_hierarchy>
    0. MEMORY: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(sort: "timeline")
       - On resume or compaction, query prior decisions, errors, plans, user prompts before asking the user — auto-captured session memory is searchable.
    1. GATHER: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute(commands, queries)
       - Primary research tool. Runs commands in parallel, auto-indexes each output, and (when queries are passed) returns matching sections in the same round trip — no follow-up search call.
       - Each command: {label: "section header", command: "shell command"}; the label becomes the FTS5 chunk title — descriptive labels improve search.
    2. FOLLOW-UP: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search(queries: ["q1", "q2", ...])
       - Multiple related questions about anything already indexed (your captures + session memory). Batch every question in one array; the ranking pipeline runs per-query and the round-trip cost is paid once.
    3. PROCESSING: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute(language, code) | mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file(path, language, code)
       - Derive answers FROM data: filter, count, aggregate, parse, transform. Only what you console.log() enters your conversation; the raw bytes stay in the sandbox.
  </tool_selection_hierarchy>

  <when_not_to_use>
    - You intend to PROCESS the output (filter, count, parse, aggregate) → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_batch_execute or mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute. Bash stays correct when you intend to OBSERVE a short fixed output (git status on a clean tree, whoami, pwd) or when you are mutating state (git, mkdir, rm, mv, navigation).
    - You want to analyze, summarize, or extract from a file → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file. Read stays correct when you intend to Edit the file (Edit needs the exact bytes in your conversation to match against).
    - WebFetch → use mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index; full network access, results indexed for mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search, raw page bytes never enter your conversation.
    - mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute and mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file for file writes → these run code in a subprocess and discard the sandbox FS; they are for analysis, processing, and computation only.
  </when_not_to_use>

    File writes use the native Write or Edit tool — mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute, mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_execute_file, and Bash subprocesses do not persist edits to the host filesystem.
    Applies to all file types: code, configs, plans, specs, YAML, JSON, markdown.
  </file_writing_policy>

    </artifact_policy>
  </output_constraints>

If a captured directive conflicts with what the user now asks, follow the user; a past phrase does not bind you.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
definition.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

definition.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
definition.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

# Advisor Tool

You have access to an `advisor` tool backed by a stronger reviewer model. It takes NO parameters -- when you call advisor(), your entire conversation history is automatically forwarded. They see the task, every tool call you've made, every result you've seen.

Call advisor BEFORE substantive work -- before writing, before committing to an interpretation, before building on an assumption. If the task requires orientation first (finding files, fetching a source, seeing what's there), do that, then call advisor. Orientation is not substantive work. Writing, editing, and declaring an answer are.

Also call advisor:
- When you believe the task is complete. BEFORE this call, make your deliverable durable: write the file, save the result, commit the change. The advisor call takes time; if the session ends during it, a durable result persists and an unwritten one doesn't.
- When stuck -- errors recurring, approach not converging, results that don't fit.
- When considering a change of approach.

On tasks longer than a few steps, call advisor at least once before committing to an approach and once before declaring done. On short reactive tasks where the next action is dictated by tool output you just read, you don't need to keep calling -- the advisor adds most of its value on the first call, before the approach crystallizes.

Give the advice serious weight. If you follow a step and it fails empirically, or you have primary-source evidence that contradicts a specific claim (the file says X, the paper states Y), adapt. A passing self-test is not evidence the advice is wrong -- it's evidence your test doesn't check what the advice is checking.

If you've already retrieved data pointing one way and the advisor points another: don't silently switch. Surface the conflict in one more advisor call -- "I found X, you suggest Y, which constraint breaks the tie?" The advisor saw your evidence but may have underweighted it; a reconcile call is cheaper than committing to the wrong branch.

- Deleting files (no rm or deletion)

- Searching code and text with powerful regex patterns
- Reading and analyzing file contents

- Use Grep for searching file contents with regex
- Use Read when you know the specific file path you need to read

tools.name: EnterWorktree
tools.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

- In a git repository: creates a new git worktree inside `.claude/worktrees/` on a new branch. The base ref is governed by the `worktree.baseRef` setting: `fresh` (default) branches from origin/<default-branch>; `head` branches from your current local HEAD
- Outside a git repository: delegates to WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks for VCS-agnostic isolation
- Switches the session's working directory to the new worktree
- Use ExitWorktree to leave the worktree mid-session (keep or remove). On session exit, if still in the worktree, the user will be prompted to keep or remove it

## Entering an existing worktree

Pass `path` instead of `name` to switch the session into a worktree that already exists (e.g., one you just created with `git worktree add`). On first entry from the launch directory, the path must appear in `git worktree list` for the repository that owns it — the current repository or, in a multi-repo workspace, a repository nested inside it; paths registered by neither are rejected. ExitWorktree will not remove a worktree entered this way; use `action: "keep"` to return to the original directory.

Switching with `path` also works when the session is already in a worktree (the previous worktree is left on disk, untouched, and only the new one is tracked for exit-time cleanup), and from agents whose working directory was pinned at launch (subagent isolation or explicit cwd). In both cases the target must be a worktree under `.claude/worktrees/` of the same repository, and from a pinned agent the switch only affects this agent, not the parent session. After a further switch, previously-visited worktrees are no longer writable — re-issue EnterWorktree with `path` to return to one.

## Parameters

- `name` (optional): A name for a new worktree. If neither `name` nor `path` is provided, a random name is generated.
- `path` (optional): Path to an existing worktree to enter instead of creating one — of the current repository, or (on first entry from the launch directory) of a repository nested inside it. Mutually exclusive with `name`.

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: SubagentHandback
tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}). The call ends your run, so do everything else first and put everything your caller needs in that one report. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

Only a report delivered through SubagentHandback reaches your caller; plain text you write at the end of your run is NOT delivered. There is no recipient parameter: the report can only go to your caller.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.   locate DEV automatically, pull config and skills, inventory every project, commit and
  push local work, pull the other machine's work, clone what is missing, report

---

# DEV sync

Eric works on a Mac and a Windows laptop. GitHub (`erash11`, all private) is the transport. This skill makes the current machine match GitHub without losing anything on either side. It is the first thing to run when sitting down at a machine.

## Step 0: find DEV (never depend on cwd)

Eric may run this from anywhere. Detect the machine and go to its DEV root:

- macOS (`uname` = Darwin): `~/DEV`
- Windows (PowerShell, or `$OS` = Windows_NT): `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV`

If that folder does not exist, stop and say so. Do not guess another location. Print the root you chose on the first line of output.

## Step 1: config and skills

These are separate repos and the other machine may have changed them:

1. `~/.claude` (repo `dotclaude`): `git pull`. If `~/.claude/machine.md` is missing, copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` for this OS. Then sync the mods: `bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\mods\mods-sync.ps1` (Windows). The folder is the list; put its one line (`mods: N loaded, N disabled, N invalid`) in the report and name any invalid mod. Then apply the 7-day rule: `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py seven-day --apply` (`portfolio_json` in `_shared/config.<platform>.json`). It pauses any project started more than 7 days ago with no receiver and no step 1 done, and prints one line plus each project paused or on the clock; put that in the report.
2. `~/.claude/skills` (repo `claude-skills`): `git pull`, then run `sync-to-codex.sh` (Mac) or `sync-to-codex.ps1` (Windows) so Codex sees the shared skills.
3. `~/.claude/global-memory` (repo `claude-global-memory`): `git pull`. **This is the only thing that carries memory between the two machines.** USER.md, MEMORY.md and the handoffs live here. `daily-backup` pushes this repo nightly, but nothing pulled it at the start of a session until this step existed, so a same-day handoff (worked on the Mac after lunch, picked up on Windows that evening) arrived with stale memory. Pull it before anything else reads it. If the pull brings in commits, say how many and name the newest, so it is visible that memory moved.

If any of the three has local uncommitted changes, commit them first with `<machine> snapshot before sync`, then pull, then push.

4. **Mirror project memory across the two slugs.** Tier A memory is keyed by a slug built from the absolute path, so every project has a Mac folder (`-Users-kristinarash-DEV-X`) and a Windows folder (`C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-X`) under `~/.claude/projects/`. dotclaude carries both to both machines, but each machine auto-loads only its own. Before this step existed, 43 memories written on the Mac never loaded on Windows (found 2026-09-24). After the pulls above, run:

   - Mac: `python3 ~/.claude/skills/dev-sync/mirror_memory.py`
   - Windows: `python $HOME\.claude\skills\dev-sync\mirror_memory.py`

   It copies files one side lacks, lets the newer version win when both have one (frontmatter `modified:`, else last commit), merges `MEMORY.md` indexes line by line, creates the twin folder when a project has memory on only one machine, and never deletes. The older side of any replaced file stays in dotclaude history. Put its summary line in the Step 4 report. If it wrote anything, commit `~/.claude` with `<machine> memory mirror` and push, so the other machine gets the result on its next sync.

   Mirroring is a union: a memory deleted on one machine comes back from the other. To retire a memory for good, delete it from both slug folders in the same commit.

Merge note for `global-memory`: `transcripts/.errors.log` and `MEMORY.md` are both append-heavy and both machines write them. On conflict, keep both sides' content rather than choosing one — these are logs, not settings, and a dropped line is a lost memory.

## Step 2: inventory (always show before changing anything)

Walk `DEV/*`, `DEV/Football/*`, and `DEV/SpecialRequests/*`. Skip `.claude`, `_tools`, `_DRIVE` (a link to the Google Drive primary storage drive, not a project; never init it, never walk into it), `token-dashboard` (someone else's remote), and any folder ending in `_OLD_merged*`. - **repo, no remote**: needs `gh repo create`
- **not a repo**: needs init + create (use the `new-project` skill's file set)

Then `gh repo list erash11 --limit 300 --json name` and list repos with no local folder. Skip: `dotclaude` (that is `~/.claude`), `SecondBrain`, `claude-skills`, `claude-memory-compiler`, `DEV`, `DexaProject`.

Eric pre-approves these operations; the inventory is for visibility, not a pause for approval, unless something looks wrong (a repo with hundreds of uncommitted files, a large file about to be added).

**Group the report by activity, not alphabetically.** Run `~/.claude/scripts/dev-activity.sh` (Mac) or `dev-activity.ps1` (Windows), which ranks repos by distinct commit days over 90 days. List the active ones individually and collapse the rest to a count: "118 dormant repos: all clean" is the useful line, not 118 names. About 14 repos are genuinely worked at any time; the rest are archives that happen to live in the same folder.

Rank by **commit days, not recency**. On 2026-09-09 a bulk migration gave 43 repos one commit each, after which every one of them looked active by any recency measure. Days-worked is not fooled by that, because a migration touches a repo once.

Nothing is archived or moved on the strength of this. Sorting is a reporting concern. Moving a dormant repo into an archive folder would break three things at once: `harvest-dev-docs` reads `<dir>/docs/*.md` without recursing, so archived repos would silently drop out of the memsearch index; KeystoneOS `projects.json`, `memory-sources.json`, `memory-index-paths.json` and `discovery-roots.json` hold DEV paths; and Tier A project memory is keyed by a slug derived from the absolute path, so moving a repo orphans its memory. Checked 2026-09-12. Do not revive the archive idea without fixing all three first.

## Step 3: apply, per repo

1. If uncommitted: put any untracked file over 95 MB and any `.env` into `.gitignore`, then `git add -A && git commit -m "<machine> snapshot before sync"`.
2. `git fetch origin` then `git merge --no-edit origin/<branch>`.
3. On conflict: keep this machine's version, save the remote version beside it as `<file>.from-mac` or `<file>.from-windows` (whichever the other machine is), stage both, commit. Never discard either side. `.DS_Store` conflicts: just delete the file.

   Save the remote side by **moving the file, never by redirecting stdout**. A
   redirect re-encodes the bytes; on Windows that silently mangles every
   non-ASCII character (an em-dash becomes `ΓÇö`) and adds a UTF-8 BOM, so the
   saved copy is corrupt and every later diff shows a phantom first-line change.

   - PowerShell: `git checkout --theirs -- <f>; Move-Item <f> <f>.from-mac; git checkout --ours -- <f>`
   - bash: `git checkout --theirs -- <f> && mv <f> <f>.from-mac && git checkout --ours -- <f>`

   Never run `git add -A` while `.git/MERGE_HEAD` exists — it stages the
   conflict markers themselves and commits a broken file. Stage only the named
   paths you just resolved.
4. `git push`.
5. Missing locally: `gh repo clone erash11/<name> DEV/<name>`.
6. No remote: `gh repo create erash11/<name> --private --source=. --push`.

Windows note: line-ending noise (`LF will be replaced by CRLF`) is normal. If a merge refuses to start because of phantom modifications, run `git add --renormalize .` and commit before merging.

Stale-lock note: if a commit or push fails with `cannot lock ref 'HEAD'`, check
`pgrep -fl git` (or `Get-Process git`) first. If no git is running and the
`.git/*.lock` file is zero bytes and older than the session, it is stale from an
interrupted run. Move it aside — do not delete it — then retry.

## Step 4: verify and report

Re-walk every repo. Report: DEV root used, config and skills pulled (yes/no), the memory-mirror summary line, repos checked, pulled, cloned, created, and any folder still dirty or unpushed. List every `.from-*` file created so Eric can reconcile them. Finish with one line: clean or not.

## Step 4b: start the project board

The live board (`project-triage/board.py`, PM system design Decision 10) writes `portfolio.json`, so it may only start on a registry that has the other machine's edits. Start it only when project-triage came through Step 3 clean: pulled, no `.git/MERGE_HEAD`, no `portfolio.json.from-*` file. Then run, from the folder holding `portfolio_json`:

- Windows: `python board.py --background`
- Mac: `python3 board.py --background`

It reuses a board already running on this machine or starts one tied to this session, opens the page, and prints `board started at <url>` or `board already running at <url>`; put that line in the report. If project-triage did not come through clean, do not start it; report `board: not started, project-triage pull unresolved` and name the conflict. Eric's `pm` (shell) and `/pm` (Claude Code) run the same command later in the day.

## Step 5: pick up where the other machine left off

Syncing git state is only half the job. The other half is loading the context that came with it, and nothing else does this — the SessionStart hook injects global memory, but project state lives in the repo, and Tier A project memory only crosses machines through the Step 1 mirror. This step is the only place that repo context gets read back in.

Do this for the repo Eric names, or the one he is in. If he has not named one, pick from the ACTIVE list in Step 2, not from all 132: take the active repo with the most recent commit and say which you chose. A dormant repo receiving one migration commit must never win this, which is exactly what picking by recency across everything would do.

1. Read `<repo>/AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md` if there is no AGENTS.md).
2. Read `<repo>/docs/STATUS.md`.
3. Read the newest file in `<repo>/docs/handoffs/`, if the folder exists and its newest file is within about two weeks.
4. If `docs/STATUS.md` does not exist in a repo that has real work in it, say so — that repo is invisible to the other machine and closeout should have created it.

Then report, in six lines or fewer, before doing any work:

```
Picking up: <repo>
Last session: <date>, <mac|windows>
Where things stand: <two lines from STATUS.md Current state>
Blocked on: <open questions, or "nothing">
Next: <top one or two from STATUS.md Next>
```

Stop there and wait for Eric to confirm or redirect. Do not start the next task off the back of STATUS.md on your own — it records where work stopped, not what he wants to do this morning.

## Do not

- Do not `rm` anything. Move to a `_to_delete` or `_OLD_*` folder if something must get out of the way.
- Do not rebase or force-push.
- Do not push DexaProject or any repo whose CLAUDE.md says its data must stay local.

---
name: closeout
description: >-
  End-of-session sign-off ritual. Sweeps loose ends, commits and pushes what needs it,
  verifies memory capture, writes a cross-harness handoff, and reports "clear to sign
  off" or what's still open. Use when the user says "/closeout", "any loose ends?", "am
  I good to sign off?", "close out for the night", "closing out", "goodnight", "wrap up
  for the day", or asks for a system health check before leaving. Do not use at the
  start of a session (use startup) or for a standalone automation health check (use
  claude-stack-doctor).
---

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

This one file serves Claude Code, Codex and Cowork (uploaded to claude.ai). Cowork has no TaskList and no Claude Code memory hooks: do what applies there and say what was skipped.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- **Registry drift.** Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py crosswalk` (`portfolio_json` is in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`). It compares `portfolio.json` with every DEV folder and Drive `01_PROJECTS` folder and only reports; it never moves anything. Do not fix drift during closeout. List each item it found under "Still open", naming any folder created this session first: that is a project started without a row, the exact way projects got lost before the 2026-10-03 organization pass. `drive_unreachable` means the Drive checks never ran; say so, do not call it clean. Cowork cannot run it; say it was skipped.
- **7-day rule.** Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py seven-day --apply`. Name any project it paused, and any project on its last two days, under "Still open" with what it still needs (a receiver, step 1). Revive with the board's status pill or `portfolio.py` once there is a first step to show.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- **Registry edits get their own commit.** In project-triage, if `git status --porcelain portfolio.json` shows a change (board edits from the day, `set-status`, `set-receiver`), commit that file alone first as `data: board edits <YYYY-MM-DD>`, then the rest. The board header's "N unpushed registry edits" counts these; a skipped one becomes a JSON merge conflict when the other machine edits too.
- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- If `~/.claude/mods` changed this session (a mod added, edited or `.disabled`), run the mods sync (`bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh` on the Mac, `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\mods\mods-sync.ps1` on Windows) and list any invalid mod under "Still open".
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours. On a Cowork-only day it may be absent; say so, it is not an error.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first. Item 1 is one concrete action (a command to run or a file to open), not a theme: it is the line `~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py` shows Eric the next morning
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

**Keep the resume cards true (PM system design Decision 9).** The live board shows each project as a card read from STATUS and the registry; if a card doesn't make sense tonight, it won't in six weeks. Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/landed.py scan --days 1` (about a minute), then `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py card-check`. It prints the card of every registry project touched today, on either machine, with its gaps. Fix each gap before the Step 2 commit:

- `STATUS has no entry dated <today>`: add `- <today>: <what happened>` under the repo's Done / Current state.
- `STATUS has no Next item`: put one concrete action first under `## Next`.
- `no next step (next_action)` (Drive-only row): set it on the board or with `portfolio.py add-update <name> "<note>" --next-action "<step>"`.
- `needs a receiver`: `portfolio.py set-receiver <name> "<who>"` (a name, or `me: <why>`). Ask Eric when it is not obvious from the session; never invent one.
- `touched but marked <status>`: revive it (`portfolio.py set-status <name> active`) or say in STATUS why a retired project was touched.

Re-run `card-check` after the fixes. Its output is the last section of the report (**Cards:**); trim to projects with work today if it is long, but never drop one that still has a gap.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped (Cowork, no hooks)
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Registry drift:** <N items, or "none"> (`portfolio.py crosswalk`)
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.

**Cards:** <`portfolio.py card-check` output, after the Step 4 fixes>
```

The cards come last on purpose: they are what the next session, on either machine, picks up from.

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

**Where everything landed.** Build that list from the ledger, not from memory: the Step 4 `landed.py scan --days 1` already refreshed it (it reads git in every DEV repo and file times on Drive and the vault, so files written by scripts and shell copies are included); run `landed.py show --days 1`. Put its project-grouped output in the report under **Landed:** (trim to the projects this session touched if it is long). The ledger lives in `~/.claude/global-memory/landed/` and is pushed with global-memory, so `/landed` on the other machine shows it too.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

---
name: interview-me
description: "End-of-workday interview in two parts: a 90-second supervisor log of operational facts (equipment, people, blockers) for the biweekly status report, then four reflection questions distilled into atomic SecondBrain notes. Use when the user types `/interview-me`, says \"interview me\", \"let's debrief\", \"end of day interview\", \"process my day\", \"wrap up today\", \"log my day\", or asks to capture their workday. Do not use for building the biweekly report itself (use status-report)."
---

# Interview Me

End-of-workday synthesis ritual. The user is a sport-science / performance analyst who writes essays connecting sport science, product strategy, and decision-making. The interview's job is to extract publishable insights, not to record what happened.

## Vault location

Use `vault_root` from the selected platform config.

**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.

- `Inbox/` — full transcripts (one per day)
- `Notes/` — atomic permanent notes (one idea per file)
- `Drafts/` — essays in progress
- `Archive/` — published
- `Templates/interview-note.md`, `Templates/permanent-note.md`
- `Inbox/status-log/` — daily supervisor fact logs (Part 0). Path key: `vault_status_log`.

---

## Part 0 — Supervisor log (90 seconds, ask first)

**Three questions, asked before the reflection questions.** Facts are easier to recall
than insight when the user is tired, and a hard 90-second opener is what makes the ritual
survivable nightly. Reflection quality does not suffer from coming second; it suffers
from the user never starting.

This part exists because `status-report` — the biweekly email to the user's supervisors —
has a sourcing gap: roughly two thirds of what belongs in that email (equipment arriving,
installs, who onboarded onto what, hallway conversations, follow-ups awaiting a reply)
appears in **no** automated source. Without a nightly log, the report has to reconstruct
two weeks from memory. With one, it mostly writes itself.

Ask all three at once. Accept short answers. Do not probe.

> Quick log first, 90 seconds. Then the usual four.
> 1. Anything arrive, get installed, or change hands today? Who's onboarding onto it?
> 2. Who did you talk to that Kenny or Chris would want to know about? Names and sport.
> 3. Waiting on anyone, or anything about to go sideways?

**Honest zero rule.** If all three are genuinely "nothing", write **no file**. A day with
no operational facts is a real day. Padding this log is worse than skipping it, because
`status-report` trusts these entries verbatim.

### Output — `{vault_status_log}/YYYY-MM-DD.md`

```markdown
---
date: YYYY-MM-DD
sports: [Football, Tennis]      # programs named in the answers; [] if none
---

## Equipment & installs
- Perch cameras installed at Foster. Football onboarding this week.

## People & conversations
- Javi (Tennis) — FirstBeat onboarding, wants a one-pager for his staff.

## Waiting on / risks
- Micah, no reply since 8/17.
```

Use the user's own words. Do not editorialize, rank, or add commentary — `status-report`
does the judgement pass later, and it needs raw facts to judge.

**Append, never overwrite.** If today's file exists (a second debrief, or a correction),
add to the existing sections rather than replacing the file.

**This log never becomes a permanent note.** It is a fact record for one downstream
consumer. Insight goes in `Notes/` via Part 1, which is why the skill's "NOT a journaling
app" rule still holds.

---

## Part 0b — Project block (30 seconds, right after Part 0)

The user works a 2-hour calendar block

404	
405	### Question 3 — Pattern (synthesis)
406	> Does anything from today connect to what you were thinking about earlier this week or recently?
407	
408	**Optional aid:** quietly Glob `Notes/*.md` modified in the last 7 days; if you find 2–3 candidates that match today's themes, name them and ask if today's experience updates them.
409	
410	### Question 4 — Essay seed (publishable insight)
411	> If you told a peer one thing about today's work, what would it be?
412	
413	This question converts experience into transferable insight. If the user gives a great one-liner — capture it verbatim as the seed for a permanent note.
414	
415	## Optional source pull-ins
416	
417	Offer when the user references them. Don't pull unprompted.
418	
419	- **Meeting referenced** ("today's call with X", "this morning's standup"):
420	  → **First, check `Inbox/meetings/` for a local summary** — Glob for files matching the date or participant. If found, read and quote from the local file (free, fast, no API call).
421	  → If not found locally, ask: *"Want me to pull from Fireflies?"* → invoke the `meeting-sync` skill to sync the latest meetings, then read the local file.
422	  → Fall back to direct `pp-fireflies` only if `meeting-sync` reports nothing matching.
423	- **Paper / article referenced:**
424	  → "Want me to pull the source from Zotero?" → use `pp-zotero-research-library` skill.
425	- **GPS / Catapult data referenced:**
426	  → "Want me to pull the underlying metric?" → use `pp-catapult-openfield-connect` skill.
427	
428	Quote sources in the note's frontmatter `source:` field or the **Evidence / origin** section.
429	
430	## Output protocol
431	
432	### Write the supervisor log (unless all three answers were nothing)
433	
434	`Inbox/status-log/YYYY-MM-DD.md` — see Part 0 for the shape. Write this **first**, before
435	the transcript, so a session that gets cut short still leaves the report its facts.
436	
437	### Always write the transcript
438	
439	`Inbox/YYYY-MM-DD-interview.md` — full Q&A, lightly cleaned. Use the `Templates/interview-note.md` skeleton. Fill in `themes`, `notes_produced`, `pulled_sources` in frontmatter.
440	
441	### Write 0–3 permanent notes
442	
443	**Bias toward fewer notes.** A vault full of mediocre notes is worse than one with three great ones. If nothing crossed the bar today, write zero — say so to the user. They will respect this.
444	
445	A note earns its place if it meets at least one of:
446	- States a transferable claim (works beyond today's context)
447	- Updates a previously held view (in which case, also update / link the old note)
448	- Names a pattern across two or more recent days
449	- Is a clean essay seed the user could draft from later
450	
451	Each note goes to `Notes/<concept-title-kebab-case>.md` with the `Templates/permanent-note.md` skeleton filled in:
452	- `created`: today's date
453	- `source`: `[[YYYY-MM-DD-interview]]`
454	- `domain`: pick from `sport-science`, `product`, `decision-making`, `leadership`, `methodology`, `personal`
455	- `tags`: free-form, but reuse existing tags from other Notes when possible
456	- Body: claim in 1–2 sentences, why it matters, evidence/origin, connections (use `[[wikilink]]` to related Notes), open questions
457	
458	### Memory bridge (when warranted)
459	
460	If the interview surfaces a **durable** fact about the user, their projects, or working style that should persist across Claude sessions:
461	- Also write a Tier A memory file via the `memory-write` skill (it derives the correct project slug from the current working directory) or update USER.md / project_*.md as appropriate.
462	- Tell the user explicitly: "Also saved this to memory as <name>."
463	- Do NOT bridge ephemeral notes. Most permanent notes stay in the vault only.
464	
465	## What NOT to do
466	
467	- **Don't pad notes with model commentary.** The user's own words and insights are the value. You are a scribe with editorial judgment, not a co-author.
468	- **Don't ask follow-up questions beyond the four** unless an answer was genuinely ambiguous and one clarification unlocks a much better note.
469	- **Don't produce a note "just to have one."** Zero notes is an honest output.
470	- **Don't break the 10–15 min budget.** Offer a follow-up session if needed.
471	- **Don't write to `Drafts/` from a daily interview.** Drafts come out of weekly synthesis, not daily capture.
472	- **Don't pad the supervisor log to make the day look productive.** `status-report` copies these entries into an email to the user's supervisors with light editing. An invented install or an inflated conversation becomes a false claim in front of Chris Ruf and Kenny Boyd. No file is the correct output for a quiet day.
473	- **Don't turn a Part 0 answer into a permanent note** unless it independently clears the Part 1 bar. Operational facts are not insight.
474	
475	## Gotchas
476	
477	- **Part 0 goes first, and that ordering is the whole design.** The ritual lapsed for 49 days in 2026 because reflection is expensive when tired. Three factual questions is a low enough floor to clear on a bad day, and a partial run that captures only the log still has value downstream. Moving Part 0 after the four questions quietly reverts the fix.
478	- **`status-report` reads this directory verbatim.** It counts logged days against the period ("N of 14 days logged") and surfaces the gap to the user. That visible gap is the intended nudge — do not backfill missing days with guesses to make the count look better.
479	- **Never hardcode the log path.** It is `vault_status_log` in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`. The vault has already moved once (off the iCloud-synced Desktop, 2026-08-14) and every hardcoded path broke.
480	- **Sports named in the answers must go in the `sports:` frontmatter array.** The status report's sport coverage panel — the reason that report exists, since it documents involvement beyond football and basketball — is assembled from this field. A conversation logged without its sport is credit the user does not get.
481	- **Append to today's file, never overwrite it.** A second debrief on the same day is common and overwriting silently deletes the first pass.
482	
483	## Weekly synthesis
484	
485	Weekly synthesis is NOT this skill's job. If the user says "weekly synthesis", "weekly review", or asks to look across the week, invoke the `weekly-review` skill — it owns the Friday ritual (themes, project status, decisions, stale action items, essay angles). This skill is strictly the daily debrief.
486	
487	## End-of-session sign-off
488	
489	Always end with a brief summary:
490	- Supervisor log: saved to `Inbox/status-log/YYYY-MM-DD.md`, or "nothing to log today"
491	- Transcript saved: `Inbox/YYYY-MM-DD-interview.md`
492	- Notes created: list with paths and one-line summaries
493	- Memory bridge: yes/no, what
494	- Any open thread to revisit tomorrow
495	
496	Keep it tight — three to five lines.
497
